title: The Great Diffusion
summary: As AI intelligence becomes a commodity, value shifts to energy, chips, settlement rails and neutral reserves. Discover CoinShares' investment thesis and the signals that could prove us wrong.
body_markdown:
## Overview


The AI arms race of 2026 occupies nearly every realm of public discourse. From the worlds of finance to politics to the shape of the future of work, much of the conversation has remained on which frontier lab (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.) will win. We at CoinShares have been closely following, and have come to a different conclusion on what winning might look like, and to that end — where exactly the value of Artificial Intelligence may end up being.


What follows is an investment thesis on the current and near-term future surrounding the development of Artificial Intelligence.


If value lands where we believe it will land — in energy, in silicon, in settlement rails, and in the neutral reserve — the consequence is favourable to digital assets, the industry we have worked in since 2013, but it does not stop there: the argument runs on into the listed equities of physical infrastructure and into compute itself as it becomes a financial asset. It is the logical real-world extension; it is the argument exiting the theoretical and coming to life.


## The AI arms race: the forest for the trees


The whitepaper


Situational Awareness


, and all that flows from it — the arms race, the focus on frontier labs, the concern over concentration, the talmudic observance of who's in first place — is worth taking note of. These developments matter to the entire world, well beyond business and finance.


But stepping back and widening the frame, a different image comes into view. The entire strategy of watching and betting on the AI arms race assumes that the winner takes all, and that the winner can extract a heavy toll. Our hypothesis is that this very prize is disappearing even as it is being chased after. Intelligence is commoditising, and this isn't mere speculation but a measurable fact. The best open models now trail the frontier by roughly four months. The cost of running AI falls by a factor of ten every year. And since February 2026, software agents have consumed more of what is being produced than humans do.


One of the biggest factors changing the shape of the race is China. Boxed out of leading-edge chips by US export controls, it knows it can't win the sprint to the frontier, so it is changing the game instead: releasing open models that are nearly as good as the frontier's, and certainly good enough for the vast majority of uses. So while everybody watches in awe and makes bets on who will win, we are asking a different question. If the AI arms race isn't what it's all about after all, where does the value go when intelligence is commoditised?


## What commoditisation sets in motion and what does it mean for crypto


Commoditisation of intelligence isn't just a pricing story. It sets in motion the remaking of five pillars of the current world order at once. Geopolitically, it dissolves the single-superpower world — and a world of several poles needs a reserve and settlement layer that no bloc owns/ Economically, the near-free coordination that flows from commoditisation shrinks the firm and creates a new actor: the software agent that contracts and pays on its own, which no bank is currently built to serve. For the state, AI erodes security and consequently the taxation consent — the two tentpoles of fiat money — and points toward a non-sovereign reserve. Physically, intelligence gets cheap but is paid for in electrons, and the megawatt doesn't commoditise. Lastly in the realm of truth, the fake becomes free, which makes proof scarce.


The five pillars taken together quickly become a sum greater than its parts, a sort of new global operating system if you will . A reserve no bloc (or single actor) can freeze. Rails that clear in seconds, price in fractions of a cent, and open an account to a counterparty with no legal personality (non-human actor). A store of value not issued by a state . A market where scarce compute can be contracted forward, collateralised and priced. Registries and signatures no single party can rewrite.


Five massive upheavals arriving from five unrelated disciplines, converging on one single specification — and it describes a layer that already exists, that no incumbent can occupy, and that has been running in production for fifteen years. A bank cannot open an account to an entity with no legal personality; a sovereign issuer cannot be neutral between blocs; a proprietary registry cannot prove it has not been rewritten. This is what we mean when we say crypto is structurally necessary to what comes next rather than merely adjacent to it. What makes it an investment case rather than a mere observation is that today's prices account for almost none of it.


## Where else the value lands


In


The Innovator's Solution


(2003), Clayton Christensen demonstrated that when a layer of a value chain commoditises, the value doesn't simply vanish. It flows to whatever remains scarce. As a historical precedent for what is happening with intelligence and infrastructure we look to the fibre glut of the 2000s and the bankruptcy of both WorldCom and Global Crossing. Those companies were wiped out but in their wake, the Magnificent Seven came into being.


If we are correct that intelligence is commoditising, value will accrue in two other places:


Upstream


, in the physical layer that can't be copied: specifically turbines, transformers, nuclear power that is under 20-year contracts, and the grid-connected megawatt with its four-to-five-year queue.


Downstream


, where distribution trumps issuance: Coinbase captures the rent on USDC, the leading regulated dollar stablecoin, while Circle, its issuer, loses 80 per cent of its stock value. And among the companies adopting AI, the 20 per cent that rebuild around capture 74 per cent of the gains (PwC, 2026).


The frontier labs, meanwhile, are analogous to the PC-era assemblers: the layer working the hardest while capturing the least. Roughly $14 of value reaches the user for every $1 of revenue the providers collect, and the rest leaves the chain entirely.


## A word on our systematic approach


We return again and again to the bet that the thesis is built on: intelligence is commoditising. For absolute clarity, we tied this bet to measurable signals with a deadline at the end of 2027. Then we say exactly what would prove us wrong.


We would treat two developments as important signposts for revisiting the thesis: the gap between open and closed models widening beyond nine to ten months for two consecutive quarters, or evidence that the frontier labs are restoring genuine pricing power on inference, with the year over year collapse in prices levelling off. Neither would invalidate the framework on its own, but either would prompt a reassessment of the assumptions underpinning it.


From the single bet we map five separate routes the value can travel, drawn from disciplines that don't ordinarily speak to one another: geopolitics, economics, the state, energy, and truth. Each route stands or falls on its own. All five arrive at the same destination — the infrastructure where the value lands.


We applied one test to everything we looked at, our own industry included: usage doesn't make the price. Stablecoins moved $33 trillion last year — more than Visa — and paid the people holding them nothing. Heavy use of a network means nothing for its token unless something specific — a fee, a buyback, a hard cap on supply — puts that value in the holder's hands. Otherwise that money ends up in someone else's pocket.


## The layers as we see them — the high-voltage grid


The infrastructure these five routes converge on is best pictured as an electrical system in six layers: the water behind the dam (bitcoin, the reserve), the turbine (miners and compute), the transmission lines (settlement), the current (stablecoins), the wholesale market (finance and credit), and the meter (proof).


We ran every asset through a single filter, a simple question: when money flows through it, does any of the money actually end up in the hands of the person holding the asset — and can that arrangement be taken away?


Out of this process emerged a ranking. Bitcoin sits alone at the top — the Constant — because its fixed supply is the one scarcity no vote can alter. Below it come the assets paying their holders today, the Real Cash Flows: the listed miners who have turned their power contracts into AI compute businesses, and the rare token whose buyback genuinely works. Next are the Dormant Assets — heavily used networks where the mechanism to pay holders exists but has never been switched on, and where we can calculate exactly what flipping it would be worth. Below those sit the Dated Asymmetries: positions whose case rests on a development we expect by a stated date. The date is not a sell trigger; it is a checkpoint. If the development has not arrived, the thesis is re-examined on the information then available, and the position stays, shrinks, or goes on what that information says — not on what we wrote in 2026. And at the bottom, External Capture: where the token keeps none of the value, we skip the token entirely and buy the listed stock that does.


## Conclusions — and the audit in one year's time


We are writing in a market trough, and it is in troughs that infrastructure gets built. But our earlier example of fibre teaches a second lesson: laying infrastructure has never enriched its holders. Only a capture mechanism does. And at the bottom of this cycle, capital has already proved it can tell the difference. In the June crash, Hyperliquid — the one token whose buyback genuinely pays its holders — printed its all-time high, and the listed miners converting their power contracts into AI business — Core Scientific, TeraWulf, IREN — outperformed bitcoin by roughly 70 percentage points.


The market has begun to price the distinction. It just hasn't applied it to the whole grid. In that gap lies our thesis.


In closing we offer ten signals, each with a validation threshold, an invalidation threshold, a named source, and a guillotine date. One of them, the master signal which tracks whether intelligence is commoditising, can break the entire thesis on its own. We are committed to returning in one year's time, at the annual review, and publishing the verdict line by line — including where we were wrong.
